concept.name: Conditional order
concept.definition: An order that is submitted to the market (or canceled) only when one or more user-defined conditions are met - typically a price, time, or event condition on the same or another instrument. Stop, trailing-stop, and if-touched orders are all specific conditional orders.
concept.intuition: It is an 'if this, then trade' instruction held by the broker: nothing exists in the market until the condition fires.
concept.mechanics: The broker or venue monitors the condition (e.g., last price of a defined contract reaching a level) and transmits the attached market or limit order when it evaluates true. Because the order is held off-book until then, trigger evaluation conventions (last trade vs. quote) and trigger latency are venue-specific.
concept.failure_modes: The held order is invisible to the market, so it has no queue priority when triggered and can miss fast moves entirely. Platform outages or a halt in the condition instrument can also prevent the trigger from ever being evaluated.
concept.misconceptions: A conditional order does not reserve execution at the condition price - after triggering it is just an ordinary market or limit order. Nor is it necessarily exchange-native; many conditional orders live only in the broker's system.
concept.example: You set a conditional order: if the S&P 500 futures fall below 5,000, submit a limit order to buy 100 shares of an index ETF at $450; the buy order only exists once the futures condition fires.
